Test3 baseline comparison: sharpness and color¶

Compares 5 candidate images against a designated baseline frame from images/test3/. Same scene assumption — differences therefore reflect focus / lens / exposure / white-balance state changes, not scene content.

Baseline: 6000011-1221-012345-4040.jpg. All metrics for the other 5 images are reported both in absolute terms and as percent-of-baseline (baseline row = 100). Per-metric direction is summarized in each section's description.

Setup¶

Metric helpers come from the shared sensor_metrics.py module.

In [1]:
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display

from sensor_metrics import (
    CHANNELS,
    load_rgb,
    luminance,
    quality_stats,
    fft_sharpness,
    color_balance_stats,
    hsv_sat_stats,
)

IMG_DIR = Path("images/test3")
BASELINE_NAME = "6000011-1221-012345-4040.jpg"

baseline_path = IMG_DIR / BASELINE_NAME
assert baseline_path.is_file(), f"baseline image missing: {baseline_path}"

all_files = sorted(IMG_DIR.glob("*.jpg"))
ordered = [baseline_path] + [p for p in all_files if p != baseline_path]


def short(p: Path, is_baseline: bool) -> str:
    return p.stem.split("-")[0] + (" (baseline)" if is_baseline else "")


labels = [short(p, p == baseline_path) for p in ordered]
images = [load_rgb(p) for p in ordered]
BASELINE_LABEL = labels[0]


def relative_to_baseline(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    base = df.loc[BASELINE_LABEL].replace(0, np.nan)
    return (df / base) * 100


print(f"Loaded {len(images)} images from {IMG_DIR.resolve()}")
print("Baseline:", BASELINE_LABEL)
for lbl, img in zip(labels, images):
    print(f"  {lbl:<22s} shape={img.shape}")

2. Sharpness metrics — formulas and direction¶

All three metrics operate on the grayscale image g(x, y) = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B.

1. Laplacian variance — laplacian_var $$ \text{laplacian\_var} = \operatorname{Var}\!\bigl(\nabla^{2} g\bigr) $$ Variance of the discrete Laplacian of the image. The Laplacian responds to edges; a focused image has strong edges, so a higher variance means sharper content.
Direction: higher = sharper (better).

2. High-frequency residual std — hf_residual_std $$ \text{hf\_residual\_std} = \operatorname{std}\!\bigl(g - G_{\sigma}(g)\bigr) $$ Standard deviation of g minus a Gaussian-blurred copy (5×5 kernel). The subtraction isolates the high-frequency band, so the std-dev is dominated by detail energy.
Direction: in same-scene / same-sensor comparison, higher = sharper (better). (Across different sensors this metric also captures sensor noise.)

3. FFT high-frequency mean — fft_highfreq_mean $$ \text{fft\_highfreq\_mean} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}|} \sum_{(u,v) \in \mathcal{H}} \bigl|\,\mathcal{F}\{g\}(u, v)\,\bigr|, \quad \mathcal{H} = \{(u,v): \sqrt{(u-c_u)^2 + (v-c_v)^2} > r\} $$ Mean magnitude of the centered FFT outside a low-frequency disk of radius r = min(H, W) / 8. The mask removes DC and very low frequencies (overall brightness, large smooth gradients) so the result is a pure high-frequency energy reading, robust to illumination shifts.
Direction: higher = sharper (better).

How to read the % table. Baseline row is 100 for every metric. Test images > 100 are sharper than baseline on that metric; < 100 are softer.

2.1 Absolute values¶

In [3]:
def all_sharpness(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    qs = quality_stats(img)
    return {
        "laplacian_var": qs["sharpness_lap_var"],
        "hf_residual_std": qs["noise_hf_std"],
        "fft_highfreq_mean": fft_sharpness(img),
    }


sharpness_abs = pd.DataFrame([all_sharpness(img) for img in images], index=labels)
sharpness_abs.index.name = "image"
sharpness_abs.round(2)

3. Color metrics — formulas and direction¶

For a same-scene comparison, the natural question is "how close is each test image's color to the baseline?" The % table is therefore a similarity reading: close to 100 = close to baseline, regardless of metric direction. Departures in either direction (above or below 100) indicate a color shift.

Per-channel mean — mean_R, mean_G, mean_B $$ \text{mean\_C} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{x,y} C(x, y), \quad C \in \{R, G, B\} $$ Average intensity of each channel (0..255). Closer to baseline = better match.

Channel ratios — R/G, B/G $$ \text{R/G} = \frac{\text{mean\_R}}{\text{mean\_G}}, \quad \text{B/G} = \frac{\text{mean\_B}}{\text{mean\_G}} $$ Classical white-balance descriptors; on a neutral scene a well-balanced sensor sits near 1.0. Closer to baseline = better match.

Gray-world deviation — gray_world_dev $$ \text{gray\_world\_dev} = \bigl\| (\bar R, \bar G, \bar B) - \bar L \cdot (1,1,1) \bigr\|_2, \quad \bar L = \tfrac{1}{3}(\bar R + \bar G + \bar B) $$ Euclidean distance of the mean RGB from the neutral-gray axis. 0 = perfectly neutral. Lower = more neutral (a smaller absolute value means a less colored image, irrespective of baseline).

CIE Lab a*, b* — Lab_a*, Lab_b*
Signed chromaticity coordinates in CIE Lab (using OpenCV's cvtColor, with the 128 neutral offset subtracted): a* is red(+) / green(−), b* is yellow(+) / blue(−). Closer to baseline = better match. Note: signed values can flip the percent ratio (e.g. baseline a=−10, test a=−5 ⇒ 50%); read together with the absolute table.

HSV mean saturation — mean_S $$ \text{mean\_S} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{x,y} S(x, y) $$ HSV S-channel mean on 0..255. Closer to baseline = better match.

3.1 Absolute values¶

In [5]:
def all_color(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    cb = color_balance_stats(img)
    sat = hsv_sat_stats(img)
    return {
        "mean_R": cb["mean_R"], "mean_G": cb["mean_G"], "mean_B": cb["mean_B"],
        "R/G": cb["R/G"], "B/G": cb["B/G"],
        "gray_world_dev": cb["gray_world_dev"],
        "Lab_a*": cb["Lab_a*"], "Lab_b*": cb["Lab_b*"],
        "mean_S": sat["mean_S"],
    }


color_abs = pd.DataFrame([all_color(img) for img in images], index=labels)
color_abs.index.name = "image"
color_abs.round(2)

3.3 Per-channel histograms vs baseline¶

For each non-baseline image: R / G / B / luminance histograms, with the baseline overlaid as a solid line and the test image as a dashed line.

In [7]:
baseline_img = images[0]
test_pairs = list(zip(labels[1:], images[1:]))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(test_pairs), 4, figsize=(16, 3 * len(test_pairs)))
if len(test_pairs) == 1:
    axes = axes[np.newaxis, :]

for r, (label, test_img) in enumerate(test_pairs):
    for c, (cname, cidx, color) in enumerate(CHANNELS):
        ax = axes[r, c]
        ax.hist(baseline_img[..., cidx].ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
                histtype="step", color=color, label="baseline")
        ax.hist(test_img[..., cidx].ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
                histtype="step", color=color, linestyle="--", label=label)
        ax.set_title(f"{label} \u2014 {cname}")
        ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax = axes[r, 3]
    ax.hist(luminance(baseline_img).ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
            histtype="step", color="k", label="baseline")
    ax.hist(luminance(test_img).ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
            histtype="step", color="k", linestyle="--", label=label)
    ax.set_title(f"{label} \u2014 luminance")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4. Conclusions and per-image report¶

Drawn from the absolute and percent-of-baseline tables above. All five test images come from the same scene as the baseline; differences reflect focus, exposure, and color-processing state rather than scene content.

Overall patterns¶

  • Sharpness. All five test images are softer than the baseline on every metric. Ranges across the test set: laplacian_var 62.7–94.1%, hf_residual_std 81.6–96.6%, fft_highfreq_mean 77.6–93.2%. All three methods agree on the ranking (6000099 worst, 6000037 best), which confirms they're measuring the same physical property and rules out single-method artifacts.

  • Exposure. Test images are darker than baseline on every channel. Magnitudes per image:

    • 6000099 — 1.2–2.4%
    • 6000037 — 2.7–3.3%
    • 6000015 — 3.0–3.7%
    • 6000209 — 3.0–3.7%
    • 6000612 — 3.6–4.2%

    Direction is consistent (always darker); magnitude varies ~1–4% across the set.

  • White balance. Channel ratios are essentially identical to baseline on all five tests (R/G 99.5–99.8 vs 100.0; B/G 100.2–100.7 vs 100.0). No detectable white-balance drift.

  • Saturation. Every test image is 23.3–36.3% more saturated than baseline (mean_S ratio 123.3 to 136.3). This is the largest and most consistent color difference in the set.

  • Lab chromaticity. Absolute shifts are small: Δa* ranges +0.39 to +0.58 (slightly more red); Δb* ranges −0.13 to −0.39 (slightly less yellow). The 300–393% relative values on Lab_a* are an artifact of dividing by a near-zero baseline (0.20); the absolute table is what to read for signed metrics.

  • Gray-world deviation. Test images are more neutral on average (64.0–80.0% of baseline). Combined with the higher saturation, this means the test frames have more colorful pixels that cancel on average — i.e. higher color variance, not a global cast.

Per-image report¶

6000015 — sharpness 89.7 / 95.5 / 89.1% (avg ~91%); saturation +31.7%; channels 3.0–3.7% darker. Mildly soft; otherwise representative of the test set.

6000037 — sharpness 94.1 / 96.6 / 93.2% (avg ~95%); saturation +23.3%; channels 2.7–3.3% darker. Best match — highest score on every sharpness metric and smallest saturation jump of the five.

6000099 — sharpness 62.7 / 81.6 / 77.6% (avg ~74%); saturation +36.3%; channels 1.2–2.4% darker. Sharpness outlier — Laplacian variance is 22.7 percentage points below the next-worst image (6000209 at 85.4%), equivalent to ~149 raw units (410.1 vs 558.8). Also the most saturated and the lightest of the five.

6000209 — sharpness 85.4 / 93.1 / 88.3% (avg ~89%); saturation +33.7%; channels 3.0–3.7% darker.

6000612 — sharpness 89.5 / 94.1 / 87.6% (avg ~90%); saturation +28.8%; channels 3.6–4.2% darker. Most exposed to the dimming shift.

Recommendation¶

  • If selecting the test image closest to baseline, pick 6000037.
  • 6000099 should be flagged or excluded — its ~23 percentage-point sharpness deficit below the next-worst image is the kind of degradation that would visibly hurt downstream object detection.
  • The +23–36% saturation gap is present on every test image and is the dominant color signal. It points to a real processing difference (gamma curve, saturation setting, or sensor-profile change) between the baseline capture and the test captures — worth tracing rather than treating as noise.
